description: We're a lank2z-led team competing in NASA Space Apps 2026. We're here to have fun, challenge ourselves, and try to be the best. Our goal is simple: create something cool.
summary:
For NASA Space Apps' Dancing with the SARs challenge, our team built APEX Terra, an interactive platform for exploring Earth and investigating real satellite radar data.

I chose the Vijayawada region in Andhra Pradesh, India, partly because my family has connections to the area and a background in agriculture. Our study covers 48.9 × 26.2 km around Vijayawada and Veeravalli—not just one village.

Using NASA–ISRO NISAR observations from October 22 and November 3, 2026, we compared about 12.8 million matching radar-grid samples and measured regional median changes of +1.23 dB (HH) and +1.58 dB (HV).

What makes Atlas interactive is that you can click a radar location to inspect its actual before-and-after HH/HV readings, compare that point with nearby and regional measurements, or draw an area to calculate statistics and export GeoTIFF data. Users can also switch radar observations, explore historical imagery through Time Lens, and travel from Earth into a connected 3D Solar System.

We added NASA GPM rainfall data for context, but we don't claim radar changes prove flooding, crop growth, or another cause. Our goal is to make real Earth science easier to explore without hiding uncertainty.
details:
APEX Terra — Project Details

Why we chose the Vijayawada region

For NASA Space Apps' Dancing with the SARs challenge, our team developed APEX Terra to make real satellite observations something people can explore and investigate themselves.

We chose a 48.90 × 26.20 km region around Vijayawada and Veeravalli in Andhra Pradesh, India, covering approximately 1,281 square kilometers.

This region has a personal connection to me through my family's background and ties to agriculture in the area. That made us especially interested in studying a landscape containing agricultural land, waterways, settlements, and surrounding communities.

Our investigation covers this entire region, not just Veeravalli. We selected one location near Veeravalli for a closer examination of individual radar measurements.

What we built

We developed APEX Terra Atlas, an interactive Earth-observation and space-exploration platform built around real satellite data.

Our main scientific investigation compares two NASA–ISRO NISAR Level-2 GCOV radar observations from October 22 and November 3, 2026.

We analyzed 12,811,774 matching radar-grid samples and measured regional median backscatter changes of +1.23 dB in HH polarization and +1.58 dB in HV polarization.

Instead of simply generating maps, we built an application where people can explore the observations and investigate the measurements behind them.

What makes APEX Terra different

Click on the map and investigate real radar measurements. One of our main features is the radar location inspector. Users can click a location within our study area and examine its actual before-and-after HH and HV readings, the measured difference, nearby observations, and regional statistics. This turns the map from a visualization into something users can investigate.

Analyze entire areas, not just individual points. Users can draw a rectangle over the study area to calculate regional statistics and export scientific results as GeoTIFF files. The map uses derived 500 m block summaries at regional zoom levels, with access to the underlying 10 m posting grid for closer inspection.

Compare satellite observations. Users can explore different radar acquisitions, switch between HH and HV polarizations, and examine spatial patterns of change. Our comparison tools help users see how measurements differ between observations.

Explore historical imagery with Time Lens. We incorporated historical optical imagery so users can explore how landscapes have appeared across different periods. These images provide geographic context and are separate from our measured NISAR radar comparison.

Explore Earth and the Solar System. We also built a connected 3D planetary experience. Users can move outward from Earth, explore celestial bodies such as Saturn, and return to their previous location on Earth. We wanted geographic exploration and space exploration to feel connected rather than like two unrelated applications.

Explore, Discover, and Research. We organized the platform around three main experiences so someone unfamiliar with radar can explore visually while more technical users can access measurements, comparisons, and scientific information.

How we built it

We used Python and geospatial-processing tools to work with NISAR Level-2 GCOV observations, compare matching geographic samples, calculate backscatter differences in decibels, and generate statistics at multiple scales.

The application uses React, TypeScript, interactive geographic visualization, a Python-based science API, and a 3D planetary exploration system.

We incorporated NASA GPM IMERG precipitation observations and ESA WorldCover land-cover data as additional environmental context.

AI-assisted tools supported programming, debugging, interface development, design, research support, scientific verification, and presentation preparation. Our satellite observations and reported scientific measurements are based on real datasets, not AI-generated radar imagery.

What we actually found

Across our approximately 1,281 km² study region, we measured median radar backscatter changes of +1.23 dB in HH and +1.58 dB in HV between the two acquisitions.

At our selected Veeravalli sample, HH backscatter changed from −8.34 dB to −5.38 dB, a difference of +2.96 dB. The surrounding 110 m square had a median change of +1.60 dB, compared with the regional median of +1.23 dB.

These results demonstrate why an individual radar measurement shouldn't automatically be treated as representative of an entire region.

We also examined NASA GPM rainfall observations for additional context. However, radar backscatter can respond to several factors, including moisture, vegetation, surface roughness, and observation geometry.

Our analysis establishes that the measured radar signal changed. It does not independently prove flooding, crop growth, or another specific environmental event.

We also account for radar speckle and spatial-resolution limitations. A 10 m posting grid does not necessarily mean independent 10 m spatial resolution.

We wanted those limitations to remain visible rather than presenting every change on the map as a confirmed environmental event.

Why it matters and what's next

We started with the Vijayawada region because of our personal connection to the area and the opportunity to investigate real satellite observations.

But APEX Terra isn't intended to stay limited to one region.

Our longer-term goal is to make it possible to explore locations around the world, investigate historical and current satellite observations, compare different datasets, and examine changes using actual scientific evidence.

We see possible applications in agriculture, water-resource research, environmental monitoring, infrastructure analysis, and education.

Future development could expand geographic coverage, integrate additional satellite missions, and provide more advanced radar-analysis tools.

We built APEX Terra because we wanted people to do more than see changes on Earth. We wanted them to be able to click on a place, investigate the measurements, and understand what the evidence actually shows.
